l: Syracuse, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Syracuse invited Pyrrhus of Epirus into Sicily when the Carthaginians were besieging it. Pyrrhus crossed from Tarentum and compelled the Carthaginians to raise the siege.

l: Carthaginians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Carthaginians repeatedly crossed into Sicily and captured Greek cities, eventually besieging Syracuse. Pyrrhus forced them to lift the siege and then, with excessive confidence, challenged their naval power.

l: Romans’ war with Pyrrhus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Romans’ war with Pyrrhus began after Tarentum invited him to intervene. Pyrrhus crossed into Italy unexpectedly, attacked the Romans when they were attacking Tarentum, and used elephants to cause panic.

l: Pyrrhus’s Italian campaign, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: During Pyrrhus’s Italian campaign, he transported cavalry, infantry, and elephants from Greece to aid Tarentum and other Italians against Rome. His unexpected arrival initially confused the Romans.

l: Pyrrhus’s Sicilian campaign, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: During Pyrrhus’s Sicilian campaign, he answered an embassy from Syracuse, crossed from Tarentum, and compelled the Carthaginians to raise their siege. He then became overconfident and sought to fight the Carthaginians at sea.

l: Lysimachus’s death, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Lysimachus’s death occurred after he crossed into Asia Minor and fought Seleucus I. He was badly defeated and killed, while his son Alexander later recovered the corpse and buried it in the Thracian Chersonese between Cardia and Pactye.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Pyrrhus withdrew from Italy to Epirus by spreading a report that aid from Macedonia and Asia Minor was coming, then defeated Antigonus and took Upper Macedonia and Thessaly. He later invaded the Peloponnese at Cleonymus’s urging, defeated the Lacedæmonians, nearly captured Sparta, and entered Argos while pursuing fugitives. Pyrrhus was killed in Argos by a tile thrown during the fighting, though the Argives said that Demeter caused his death in the form of a woman. His death marked the end of the glory of Epirus.

l: Pyrrhus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Pyrrhus withdrew from Italy by spreading a report that Macedonians and other forces from Asia Minor would come to his aid. He later defeated Antigonus’s troops and foreign Galatian contingent, took Upper Macedonia and Thessaly, invaded the Peloponnese at Cleonymus’s urging, defeated the Lacedæmonians, and nearly captured Sparta. He was killed in Argos after entering the city with pursuing troops.

l: Tarentum, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Tarentum was where Pyrrhus sailed after his defeat with the remnant of his fleet. Pyrrhus later summoned the chief men of Tarentum to hear that aid would come to him.

l: Romans, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Romans were expected not to let Pyrrhus leave Italy without opposition. They remained quiet after hearing that Macedonians and other forces from Asia Minor would come to Pyrrhus’s aid, allowing him to cross to the Ceraunian Mountains.

l: Antigonus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Antigonus failed to bring reinforcements to Pyrrhus in Italy, after which Pyrrhus proclaimed war against him. Pyrrhus defeated Antigonus’s troops and the Galatian contingent with him, pursued them to the maritime cities, and took Upper Macedonia and Thessaly.

l: Macedonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Macedonians were defeated by Pyrrhus, whose victory brought him mastery of Upper Macedonia. Their arms were hung up to Zeus of the Macedonians at Dodona, with an inscription describing them as spoils taken from Macedonia.

l: Epirus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Epirus was Pyrrhus’s homeland and the place to which he did not return after entering the Peloponnese. The death of Pyrrhus is presented as the end of the glory of Epirus.

l: Italy, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: After Pyrrhus suffered a defeat in Italy, he escaped by crossing toward the Ceraunian Mountains under cover of night. The failure to receive reinforcements for the war in Italy became one of his main charges against Antigonus.

l: Cleonymus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Cleonymus, a Lacedæmonian excluded from the kingship after a dispute with Areus, called Pyrrhus into the country in an attempt to obtain the kingdom. He had earlier persuaded Pyrrhus to leave Macedonia and come to the Peloponnese.

l: Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Lacedæmonians had formerly refused to admit that they could be conquered by a land army, despite earlier reverses. When Pyrrhus invaded, they fought with allies from Argos and Messene, but Pyrrhus defeated them and came close to taking Sparta.

l: Peloponnese, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Pyrrhus entered the Peloponnese after Cleonymus persuaded him to leave Macedonia. He ravaged Lacedæmonian territory, nearly captured Sparta, and later arrived at Argos.

l: Argos, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Pyrrhus arrived at Argos while Antigonus was preparing to move against Spartan territory. After being victorious, Pyrrhus pursued fugitives into the city, where his forces became dispersed and fought in temples, houses, and alleys.

l: Sparta, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Pyrrhus conquered the Lacedæmonians and came within an ace of taking Sparta at his first assault. He then ravaged its territory and took much booty, while the Spartans prepared for a siege behind trenches, palisades, and other defenses.

l: Demeter, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Argives said that Demeter, appearing in the form of a woman, caused Pyrrhus’s death by throwing a tile. A temple to Demeter was erected on the spot where Pyrrhus died, in accordance with an oracle.

l: war in Italy, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The war in Italy ended with Pyrrhus’s defeat and his flight from the country. His failure to receive reinforcements for this war was the principal reason he later declared war against Antigonus.

l: battle of Pyrrhus against Antigonus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: In the battle against Antigonus, Pyrrhus defeated Antigonus’s own troops and the foreign Galatian contingent accompanying them. The victory gave him Upper Macedonia and Thessaly, and the captured Galatian and Macedonian arms were dedicated in temples.

l: death of Pyrrhus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Pyrrhus died during the fighting in Argos after he entered the city while pursuing fugitives. The account says that a woman threw the fatal tile, while the Argives attributed the act to Demeter appearing as a woman.

l: glory of Epirus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The glory of Epirus ended with the death of Pyrrhus. His death is compared with the supernatural ends attributed to other members of the line of the Æacidæ.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The unit describes temples, statues, paintings, monuments, and traditions in Athens, including those connected with Demeter, Triptolemus, Athene, Theseus, Zeus, and other gods and heroes. It recounts competing Argive and Athenian traditions about Triptolemus and the teaching of agriculture, as well as stories of Theseus, the Amazons, the Persian wars, and the recovery of Theseus's bones. The Painted Chamber commemorates Athenian victories at Œnoe and Marathon and displays scenes from Greek mythology and history. The account concludes with the precinct and temple of Olympian Zeus, including monuments erected by Adrian and traditions concerning Deucalion and the flood.

l: Athens, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Athens contains the Odeum, the Painted Chamber, numerous temples, monuments, statues, and public buildings described throughout the unit. Its traditions and monuments emphasize its antiquity, religious practices, victories over the Persians, and devotion to figures such as Theseus and Athene.

l: Demeter, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Demeter is worshipped in a temple near the Nine Springs. According to different traditions, she received information about the rape of Proserpine and taught Triptolemus and others how to sow corn.

l: Proserpine, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Proserpine has a temple near the Nine Springs, alongside the temple of Demeter. Her rape is reported in the traditions concerning Triptolemus and the rites associated with Demeter.

l: Triptolemus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Triptolemus has a statue in the temple near the Nine Springs and another statue in front of the Eleusinium. The Athenians identify him as the son of Celeus and the first person to sow corn, while other traditions make him the son of Ocean and Earth, or of Dysaules or Rharus.

l: Poseidon, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Poseidon is said in a Libyan tradition to be the father of Athene, whose eyes are therefore grey like his. He is also identified as the father of Cercyon in the account given by Choerilus.

l: Marathon, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Marathon is the plain from which the hero Marathon is said to have taken his name. The Painted Chamber depicts the battle there, including the Athenians, the Plataeans, Callimachus, Miltiades, and the hero Echetlus.

l: Persians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Persians are depicted in the Painted Chamber being defeated at Marathon, driven into the marsh, and killed while attempting to board their ships. They also landed at the Acropolis and killed Athenians who had fortified it with wooden palisades.

l: Athene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Athene has a statue in the temple of Hephaestus and is represented with grey eyes in accordance with a Libyan tradition about her parentage. She is also depicted in the Painted Chamber with Theseus and Hercules, and her shield shows the battle between Theseus and the Amazons.

l: Theseus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Theseus is associated with the temple bearing his name, where paintings show his battles with the Amazons and the Centaurs and Lapiths. He is said to have recovered Minos's ring from the sea and received a golden crown from Amphitrite, but later was imprisoned in Thesprotia and killed on Scyrus; Cimon subsequently brought his bones to Athens.

l: Amazons, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Amazons are depicted fighting Theseus and the Athenians in the Painted Chamber and on Athene's shield. Although they suffered defeats at the hands of Hercules and the Athenians, they later fought at Ilium and against other Greeks.

l: Miltiades, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Miltiades is shown prominently among the Athenian commanders in the Painted Chamber's depiction of Marathon. His son Cimon later drove the inhabitants of Scyrus away and brought Theseus's bones to Athens.

l: Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Zeus is associated with the ancient temple of Olympian Zeus, a shrine of Cronos and Rhea, and a grove dedicated to Earth under the title of Olympian. A statue of Zeus is also said to have given a sign of future prosperity to Seleucus when sacrificial wood moved toward it and ignited.

l: Temple of Theseus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Temple of Theseus contains paintings of the Athenians fighting the Amazons, Theseus fighting the Centaurs and Lapiths, and Theseus recovering Minos's ring from the sea. It is also connected with varying accounts of Theseus's adventures and death.

l: Adrian, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Adrian built the temple of Olympian Zeus at Athens and placed in it a colossal ivory-and-gold statue of Olympian Zeus. He also erected temples to Hera and Pan-Hellenian Zeus and a temple for all the gods, as well as the Adrian gymnasium.

l: temple of Olympian Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Olympian Zeus temple was built by Adrian and contained a colossal statue of Olympian Zeus, numerous statues of Adrian and of the empire's colonial cities, and ancient shrines to Zeus, Cronos, Rhea, and Earth. Its precinct included traditions about Deucalion's flood, a cavity into which offerings are cast, statues of Isocrates and Persians, and other monumental structures.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The unit describes temples, statues, rivers, monuments, and paintings in Athens, including the Lyceum, the theatre of Dionysus, the temple of Æsculapius, and the Acropolis. It recounts myths involving Theseus, Dionysus, Hippolytus, Phædra, Ægeus, Odysseus, and other Greek figures. It also narrates Sulla’s capture and punishment of Athens after Aristion allied the city with Mithridates against the Romans. The unit praises Euripides, Sophocles, and Æschylus as major dramatists and records various artistic works and historical traditions preserved in Athens.

l: Athens, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Athens contained numerous temples, statues, paintings, tombs, and other works of art, including the theatre of Dionysus, the temple of Æsculapius, and the Acropolis. It suffered severely when Sulla captured it after its conflict with the Romans, but flourished again under the Emperor Adrian.

l: Athenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The Athenians regarded the Ilissus as sacred to several gods and maintained various shrines and monuments throughout the city. They supported Aristion’s preference for Mithridates only among the democracy and fiercer spirits, while more respectable Athenians joined the Romans; later they erected a brazen lioness in honour of Leæna.

l: Ilissus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The Ilissus was one of the rivers of Attica and was said to be the place where Orithyia was carried off by the North Wind. The Athenians considered it sacred to several gods, and the river bordered the white-marble stadium built by Herodes.

l: Praxiteles, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Praxiteles was credited with a Satyr and with the design of the statue of Brauronian Artemis. He reportedly prized his Satyr highly and accidentally revealed to Phryne that his finest works were the Satyr and Cupid.

l: Dionysus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Dionysus had shrines and statues in the oldest temple of Dionysus at the theatre, including works by Eleuthereus and Alcamenes. He was said to have taken the drunken Hephæstus to Heaven, and to have carried off Ariadne after Theseus abandoned her.

l: theatre of Dionysus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The theatre contained the most ancient temple of Dionysus, two shrines, statues, and paintings depicting myths involving Dionysus, Hephæstus, Pentheus, Lycurgus, Ariadne, and Theseus. Statues of tragic and comic dramatists, including Euripides, Sophocles, and Æschylus, were also displayed there.

l: Sulla, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Sulla led the Roman attack that captured Athens after the city supported Mithridates. He shut Athenian adversaries in the Ceramicus, ordered them to be decimated by lot, and was blamed for treating many Athenians with exceptional savagery; he also burned the original imitation of Xerxes’ tent.

l: Mithridates, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Mithridates was king of the barbarians near the Euxine Sea and employed Aristion as an ambassador to the Greek states. He fought the Romans, sending Archelaus and Taxilus as generals, and gained the support of part of Athens.

l: Aristion, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Aristion, employed by Mithridates as an ambassador, persuaded the Athenian democracy and fiercer spirits to prefer Mithridates’ friendship to that of the Romans. After the Roman victory he fled to the temple of Athene, but Sulla tore him away and put him to death.

l: Romans, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The Romans were supported by the more respectable Athenians during the conflict caused by Aristion’s alliance with Mithridates. Their forces defeated the Athenians and Mithridates’ generals, captured Athens, and besieged the Piræus.

l: Euripides, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Euripides was regarded as one of the great lights of Tragedy. His statue stood among those of tragic and comic dramatists in the theatre.

l: Sophocles, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Sophocles was regarded as one of the great lights of Tragedy, and his statue stood in the theatre. After his death, a Lacedæmonian leader reportedly dreamed that Dionysus commanded him to honour the new Siren, which was understood to refer to Sophocles and his plays.

l: Æschylus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Æschylus was regarded as one of the great lights of Tragedy, and his statue was completed long after his death. He said that Dionysus appeared to him in a dream and commanded him to write tragedy, after which he found the work easy.

l: temple of Æsculapius, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The temple of Æsculapius contained statues of the god and his sons, paintings, and a spring in which Halirrhothius was said to have drowned. It also displayed a Sarmatic coat of mail, prompting an account of Sarmatian armour made from horse hoofs.

l: Hippolytus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Hippolytus had a sepulchre before the temple of Themis, and his death was attributed to the curses of his father, Theseus. He was sent to Pittheus at Træzen to be brought up and rule there, and Phædra’s unsuccessful love for him led to his death.

l: Phædra, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Phædra first saw Hippolytus at Træzen and became desperately enamoured of him. After he rejected her, she contrived his death; a perforated myrtle at Træzen was said to have been altered by her in her lovesickness.

l: Acropolis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The Acropolis had only one approach because it was otherwise precipitous and walled off. Its entrance included marble-roofed vestibules, the shrine of Wingless Victory, paintings, a Hermes called Propylæus, and the Graces attributed to Socrates.

l: Ægeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Ægeus was said to have drowned himself after seeing the ship returning from Crete with black sails, believing that Theseus had died. The Athenians maintained a hero-chapel in his memory, and the sea was visible from the shrine of Wingless Victory where he was said to have drowned.

l: Odysseus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Odysseus appeared in paintings at the Acropolis taking the Palladium from Ilium. He was also depicted suddenly appearing while Nausicaa and her maids were bathing in the river, as Homer described.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The unit describes artworks and religious customs in Athens, including representations of Athene, Zeus, Poseidon, and mythological figures. The Parthenon contains scenes of Athene's birth and her contest with Poseidon for Attica, as well as a chryselephantine statue of Athene. It also recounts Athenian rites involving Zeus the Guardian of the city and explains the worship of Apollo as the Averter of Locusts. The text emphasizes the Athenians' exceptional zeal for religion and describes several votive offerings and statues.

l: Athene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Athene is portrayed striking Marsyas because he took up her flutes after she wished them thrown away. She is also shown springing from the head of Zeus, displaying the olive tree, and competing with Poseidon for the soil of Attica.

l: Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Zeus is represented as the recipient of Earth’s supplication for rain and as the Guardian of the city in a statue by Leochares. At the altar of Zeus the Guardian of the city, barley is placed unwatched so that a sacrificial ox eats it, after which an ox-killer throws an axe at the ox and flees; the axe is then brought to court as the defendant.

l: Athenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Athenians are said to have greater zeal for religion than any other Greeks. They first called Athene the worker, first worshipped the mutilated Hermae, and kept a God of the Zealous in their temple.

l: Poseidon, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Poseidon is represented showing water in the contest with Athene for the soil of Attica. The contest is depicted behind the Parthenon, opposite the representation of Athene’s birth.

l: the Parthenon, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Parthenon depicts Athene’s birth on its front gables and the contest between Poseidon and Athene for the soil of Attica behind them. Its principal statue is made of ivory and gold and shows Athene with a helmet, tunic, shield, spear, Victory, and other associated figures; the base depicts the birth of Pandora.

l: the contest between Poseidon and Athene for the soil of Attica, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The contest between Poseidon and Athene for the soil of Attica is depicted behind the Parthenon, with Athene showing the olive tree and Poseidon showing water.

l: the statue of Athene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The statue of Athene is full length and made of ivory and gold. It has a tunic reaching to the feet, Medusa’s head on the breast, a four-cubit Victory in one hand, a spear in the other, a shield at the feet, and a dragon near the spear that may be Erichthonius; its base depicts Pandora’s birth.

l: Apollo, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: A brazen statue of Apollo outside the Parthenon is said to be by Phidias and is called Apollo Averter of Locusts. The name refers to the god’s removal of locusts when they destroyed the land, although the manner in which he did so is not known.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The unit describes monuments and dedications in the Acropolis at Athens, including statues and paintings honoring Pericles, Xanthippus, Olympiodorus, and others, as well as sanctuaries of Athene. It recounts the decline of Greek independence after the battle of Chaeronea, the Macedonian occupation of Athens, the revolt led by Leosthenes, and Olympiodorus’s later liberation of the city. It also explains the Erechtheum, the ancient worship of Athene, and several Athenian legends involving Poseidon, Erechtheus, Theseus, and the Marathonian bull.

l: Olympiodorus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Olympiodorus was honored for reviving Athenian hopes after repeated failures and was elected general when the Athenians remembered the fame of their ancestors. He defeated the Macedonians, captured the Museum, recovered the Piraeus and Munychia, and defeated Macedonian forces at Eleusis; he also secured Aetolian help against Cassander and aided the Phocians at Elatea. Athens honored him in the Acropolis and Prytaneum, Eleusis displayed a painting of him, and the Phocians erected a bronze statue to him at Delphi.

l: Athene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Athene was worshipped throughout Athens and Attica, with her most sacred statue standing in the Acropolis, formerly called the Polis. The Athenians said that this statue had fallen from heaven, and they also said that Athene used the olive tree as proof of her claim to the country in her contest with Poseidon. Her temple contained the sacred olive, ancient statues, votive offerings, and a continually burning golden lamp made by Callimachus.

l: Athenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Athenians rebelled against Macedonian rule after Alexander’s death and urged other Greek cities to join them, choosing Leosthenes as generalissimo. They later endured Macedonian garrisons and the rule of leaders imposed or supported by Cassander, including Demetrius son of Phanostratus and Lachares. Under Olympiodorus they defeated the Macedonians, recovered Athens, the Piraeus, and Munychia, and honored their fallen and victorious leaders.

l: Greeks, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Greeks suffered a general loss of freedom after the battle of Chaeronea, which made slaves of both those who were absent and those who fought against the Macedonians. Several Greek cities joined the Athenians against Macedonia, while the Bœotians in the former Theban territory supported the Macedonian interest.

l: Macedonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Macedonians gained control over much of Greece after the battle of Chaeronea and occupied Athens with garrisons at Munychia, the Piraeus, and the long walls. They later held the Museum until Olympiodorus defeated them and captured it, after which Athens was delivered from their control.

l: Athens, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Athens suffered the loss of its islands and naval supremacy after Philip’s treaties and later endured Macedonian occupation, imposed rulers, and the rule of Lachares. Demetrius son of Antigonus eventually overthrew Lachares, but retained the Piraeus and fortified the Museum before Olympiodorus liberated the city. The unit also describes Athens’s Acropolis, temples, monuments, legends, and religious customs.

l: Acropolis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Acropolis contained statues of Pericles, Xanthippus, Anacreon, Io, Callisto, and Olympiodorus, along with paintings and monuments commemorating mythic and historical battles. It housed the temples of Athene Polias and Pandrosus, the ancient statue of Athene, sacred offerings, the golden lamp of Callimachus, and the olive associated with Athene’s contest with Poseidon. Olympiodorus and Leocritus were among those honored there.

l: Piraeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Piraeus was among the Athenian possessions taken or controlled by Macedonian forces. Demetrius son of Antigonus did not immediately return it after Lachares fled, but Olympiodorus later recovered it along with Munychia.

l: Museum, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Museum stood on a hill opposite the Acropolis, within the old city walls, at a place associated with Musaeus. Demetrius son of Antigonus fortified it, and it became a refuge for the Macedonians until Olympiodorus captured it after defeating them.

l: Attica, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Attica included the fortified places of Panactus, Salamis, Munychia, the Piraeus, and Eleusis mentioned in the unit’s account of Macedonian control and Athenian resistance. It was also the setting of the Marathonian bull, which Theseus was said to have driven to the Acropolis and sacrificed to Athene.

l: Eretheum, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Erechtheum contained an altar of Supreme Zeus, altars to Poseidon, Erechtheus, Butes, and Hephaestus, and paintings of the family of Butes. It also had a well said to contain seawater, a roaring sound when the south wind blew, and a trident-shaped mark in the rock attributed to Poseidon.

l: battle of Chaeronea, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The battle of Chaeronea is described as the beginning of sorrows for the Greeks. Its aftermath brought enslavement and Macedonian domination to both Greeks who had not attended the battle and those who had fought against the Macedonians.

l: Lamian War, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: After Alexander’s death, the Athenians and several allied Greek cities took up arms against Macedonian control. Leosthenes led the coalition and initially achieved notable successes, but his death caused widespread discouragement and contributed to the failure of the effort.

l: Macedonian occupation of Athens, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Macedonian forces first occupied Munychia and later the Piraeus and the long walls. After Cassander became king, he captured Panactus and Salamis and supported rulers over Athens, while Demetrius son of Antigonus later maintained a garrison and fortified the Museum.

l: Olympiodorus's liberation of Athens, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Olympiodorus led old men and young men against the Macedonians and defeated them in battle. He captured the Museum, thereby freeing Athens from the Macedonians, and later recovered the Piraeus and Munychia and defeated Macedonian forces at Eleusis.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The unit describes Athenian statues, temples, courts, monuments, tombs, and sacred places, especially around the Acropolis, the Areopagus, and the Academy. It explains traditions concerning Athene, Apollo, Pan, the Venerable Ones, and various heroes, as well as the origins and functions of Athenian law-courts. It records the tombs and memorials of Athenian soldiers, generals, statesmen, philosophers, and artists, including Thrasybulus, Pericles, Plato, and Lycurgus. It also recounts historical conflicts involving the Persians, Lacedæmonians, Bœotians, Macedonians, and others.

l: Athene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Athene is represented by several famous works in Athens, including a brazen statue made by Phidias from Persian spoil and the Lemnian Athene, also made by Phidias. Her statue called the Lemnian Athene was dedicated by the people of Lemnos. The Acropolis also contains an altar of Athene Area and an altar of Athene Goddess of Horses near Colonus.

l: Phidias, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Phidias made the brazen statue of Athene from spoil taken from the Persians who landed at Marathon. He also made the Lemnian Athene, described as one of his finest works. The carvings on the shield of the brazen Athene were said to be by Mys, with Parrhasius drawing their outlines for him.

l: Persians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The Persians who landed at Marathon were defeated, and spoil taken from them was used to make Phidias's brazen statue of Athene. Philippides reported that the Lacedæmonians delayed marching against the Persians because they would not campaign until the moon was full.

l: battle of Marathon, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The Battle of Marathon is associated with the Persian spoil used for Phidias's brazen statue of Athene. The Athenians who fought there had tombs on the spot because of their valour, unlike the other Athenian war dead buried on the road to the Academy.

l: brazen statue of Athene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The brazen statue of Athene was made by Phidias from spoil taken from the Persians who landed at Marathon. Its shield depicted the battle of the Lapithæ with the Centaurs and other scenes, and its spearpoint and helmet plume could be seen from Sunium by sailors approaching Athens.

l: Pericles son of Xanthippus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: A statue of Pericles son of Xanthippus stood among the votive offerings on the Acropolis. He also had a tomb on the road to the Academy, near the tombs of Thrasybulus, Chabrias, and Phormio. Lycurgus was said to have put 6,500 talents more into the public treasury than Pericles had collected.

l: Acropolis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The Acropolis contained famous votive offerings, including the brazen statue of Athene, a brazen chariot made from spoil of the Bœotians and Chalcidians, and statues of Pericles and the Lemnian Athene. Its walls, except for the part built by Cimon son of Miltiades, were said to have been drawn out by the Pelasgians Agrolas and Hyperbius.

l: Cimon, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Cimon son of Miltiades built part of the walls of the Acropolis. He also led picked Athenian men sent to aid the Lacedæmonians during the revolt of the Helots, though the Lacedæmonians sent them back because of suspicion.

l: Pan, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Pan was said to have met Philippides near the Parthenian forest while Philippides was carrying a message to Lacedæmon. Pan declared that he was friendly to the Athenians and would help them at Marathon, and the Athenians honoured him for this message.

l: Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The Lacedæmonians delayed marching against the Persians at Marathon because their custom was not to campaign until the moon was full. They later requested aid from the Athenians during the Helot revolt but sent Cimon's picked men back under suspicion. At Tanagra they defeated the Athenians after the Thessalians betrayed them, but they were later completely routed by the Bœotians at Leuctra.

l: the Areopagus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The Areopagus was so called because Ares was first tried there, and Orestes was also said to have been tried there for killing his mother. Those acquitted before it offered sacrifices at the nearby temple of the Venerable Ones, and two white stones used by defendants and plaintiffs were called Rigour-of-the-law and Impudence. Ephialtes was remembered as having tried to discredit the legislation of the Areopagus.

l: Academy, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The Academy had once belonged to a private man but had become a gymnasium. Near it were precincts of Artemis, an altar of Eros, an altar of Prometheus from which runners carried lighted torches, altars of the Muses, Hermes, Athene, and Hercules, and the tomb of Plato. The road to the Academy also contained many tombs of Athenian soldiers and notable men.

l: Thrasybulus son of Lycus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Thrasybulus son of Lycus had the first tomb on the road to the Academy. He was described as one of the most famous Athenians and was praised for marching from Thebes with only sixty men, overthrowing the Thirty Tyrants, and persuading the divided Athenians to reconcile.

l: Plato, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Plato's tomb was near the Academy. The text says that the Deity foretold Plato would become most excellent in Philosophy, and that Socrates received this indication in a dream of a swan flying into his bosom on the night before Plato was to become his pupil.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: The unit describes the townships, mountains, monuments, temples, and traditions of Attica, including Marathon, Brauron, Rhamnus, Oropus, and Salamis. It recounts the Persian defeat at Marathon and the honours paid to the Athenian dead, Echetlæus, and Hercules. It describes Nemesis at Rhamnus, Amphiaraus’s temple and dream oracle at Oropus, and the religious sites and traditions associated with Salamis and Ajax. It also records traditions concerning islands, heroes, ancient kings, and notable tombs and bodies.

l: Attica, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Attica contains numerous townships, mountains, islands, temples, altars, tombs, and monuments. Its townships include Alimus, Zoster, Prasiæ, Marathon, Brauron, Rhamnus, Oropus, and others, while its mountains include Pentelicus, Parnes, Hymettus, and Anchesmus.

l: Marathon, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Marathon lies about equidistant from Athens and Carystus in Eubœa and was the place where the Persians landed and were defeated. It has the tomb of the Athenians who died in the battle, a monument to Miltiades, a monument for the Platæans and their slaves, a lake into which many fleeing Persians fell, and a cave of Pan on a nearby mountain.

l: Persians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: The Persians landed at Marathon but were defeated and lost some ships while retreating. Many fugitives fell into Marathon’s muddy lake, and those who landed at Rhamnus brought Parian marble for a victory trophy before they had conquered Athens.

l: battle of Marathon, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: The battle was fought at Marathon, where the Athenians defeated the Persians. The Athenians buried their own dead and the dead of the Platæans and their slaves, honoured the fallen as heroes, and said that Echetlæus, a rustic figure who killed Persians with a ploughshare, appeared during the fighting.

l: Athenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: The Athenians honoured the heroes of Marathon, Marathon himself, Hercules, and Echetlæus, and erected a white-stone trophy at the place where Echetlæus appeared. They also controlled Oropus after Philip gave it to them, paid divine honours to Ajax and Eurysaces, and maintained religious and historical traditions at Salamis and elsewhere in Attica.

l: Oropus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Oropus lies near the sea between Attica and Tanagra and contains the temple of Amphiaraus, whose worship began there. Near the temple is a fountain into which people throw gold or silver coins after being cured through the oracle.

l: Nemesis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Nemesis has a temple at Rhamnus and is described as especially implacable toward haughty men. Phidias made her statue from the Parian marble brought by the Persians for a projected trophy, depicting her with a crown, figures of stags, small Victories, an apple branch, and a bowl.

l: Amphiaraus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Amphiaraus was said to have been swallowed by the earth with his chariot while fleeing from Thebes, though this was said to have happened at Harma rather than Oropus. At Oropus he is worshipped as a god, has a temple and a white-stone statue, and gives divine direction through dreams after worshippers perform sacrifices and sleep wrapped in a ram’s skin.

l: Salamis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Salamis lies opposite Eleusis and extends toward Megaris; it has ruins of a market, a temple of Ajax, and a statue of Ajax made of ebony. It also contains temples of Artemis and Cychreus, and a trophy for the naval victory won by Themistocles for the Greeks.

l: Ajax, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Ajax was associated with Salamis, where he had a temple and an ebony statue, and the Athenians paid divine honours to him and to Eurysaces. A stone near the harbour was shown as the place where Telamon sat watching Ajax’s sons sail to Aulis, and the people of Salamis said that a distinctive white-and-red flower first appeared on the island after Ajax’s death.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVII. .. And as you go a little further is the grove of the hero Lacius, who
s: The unit describes the grove of the hero Lacius and nearby religious sites, tombs, and monuments along the road near the Cephisus. It recounts how Demeter gave Phytalus a fig tree after being received into his house, and how Theseus was purified at an altar to Milichian Zeus after killing the progeny of Phytalus. It also mentions the temple of Cyamites, whose name may refer either to the first planter of beans or to a hero. Near Athens, a temple originally dedicated to Apollo later contained statues of Demeter, Proserpine, Athene, and Apollo.

l: Lacius, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVII. .. And as you go a little further is the grove of the hero Lacius, who
s: Lacius is identified as a hero who gives his name to a township.

l: grove of Lacius, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVII. .. And as you go a little further is the grove of the hero Lacius, who
s: The grove of Lacius lies a little farther along the road and is associated with the hero Lacius. A tomb of Nicocles of Tarentum, an altar to Zephyrus, and a temple of Demeter and Proserpine are located there.

l: Demeter, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVII. .. And as you go a little further is the grove of the hero Lacius, who
s: Demeter is honored with Proserpine, Athene, and Poseidon in a temple in the grove of Lacius. She received Phytalus into her house and gave him a fig tree in return; she is also represented in a temple that was originally dedicated to Apollo.

l: Proserpine, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVII. .. And as you go a little further is the grove of the hero Lacius, who
s: Proserpine is honored with Demeter, Athene, and Poseidon in the temple in the grove of Lacius. A statue of Proserpine also stands in a temple that was originally built to Apollo.

l: Phytalus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVII. .. And as you go a little further is the grove of the hero Lacius, who
s: Phytalus received Demeter into his house, and she gave him the fig tree. His tomb bears an inscription commemorating this event and the lasting fame of his race; Theseus was later purified after slaying Phytalus's progeny.

l: Cephisus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVII. .. And as you go a little further is the grove of the hero Lacius, who
s: Cephisus is a river crossed along the route. Near it are statues of Mnesimaches and his son, who is shown cutting off his hair as a votive offering to the river, and on the other side is an ancient altar to Milichian Zeus.

l: Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVII. .. And as you go a little further is the grove of the hero Lacius, who
s: Milichian Zeus has an ancient altar on the far side of the Cephisus. Theseus was purified there after slaying the progeny of Phytalus.

l: Theseus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVII. .. And as you go a little further is the grove of the hero Lacius, who
s: Theseus was purified at the altar of Milichian Zeus after killing the progeny of Phytalus. He had also killed other robbers, including Sinis, who was related to him through Pittheus.

l: temple of Cyamites, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVII. .. And as you go a little further is the grove of the hero Lacius, who
s: The temple of Cyamites is a small temple beside the road. The account does not establish whether Cyamites was the first person to sow beans or a hero whose name became associated with the temple.

l: Athens, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVII. .. And as you go a little further is the grove of the hero Lacius, who
s: Athens is the place to which Chalcinus and Daetus were permitted to return after consulting the god, and the Athenians made them citizens. The unit also describes religious sites and monuments along the road near Athens.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The unit describes the sacred Rheti, Eleusis, its traditions concerning Demeter, Proserpine, Eumolpus, Triptolemus, and the Eleusinian Mysteries, as well as the boundary with Bœotia. It recounts the battle between the Eleusinians and Athenians, after which Eleusis became politically Athenian while retaining control of its Mysteries. It then traces the history, monuments, traditions, and rival accounts of Megara, including its relations with Pandion, Nisus, Thebes, and Alcathous. The account also discusses Theseus's exploits and several heroic tombs and sanctuaries around Eleusis and Megara.

l: Rheti, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The Rheti flow like rivers but contain seawater, and they were thought possibly to run underground from the Euripus near Chalcis. They were sacred to Proserpine and Demeter, and only their priests could catch fish in them; in earlier times they marked the boundary between the Eleusinians and Athenians.

l: Proserpine, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The Rheti were sacred to Proserpine, and the place called Erineus was where Pluto was said to have descended after carrying her off. Her rape was also associated with Demeter's sitting at the Well of Flowers in the guise of an old woman.

l: Demeter, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The Rheti were sacred to Demeter, and her rites with Proserpine were performed by the daughters of Celeus. After Proserpine's rape, Demeter was said to have sat at the Well of Flowers disguised as an old woman before being taken in by the daughters of Celeus.

l: Eleusinians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The Eleusinians fought the Athenians, and peace left them Athenian in other respects while allowing them private management of the Mysteries. Their women were said to have first danced and sung to Demeter at the Well of Callichorus, and their territory contained temples, tombs, and other sacred sites.

l: Athenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The Athenians fought the Eleusinians and thereafter included Eleusis within the Athenian political community while leaving the Eleusinians control of their Mysteries. They also claimed that Megara had originally belonged to them and later lost it to the Peloponnesians.

l: Eumolpus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Eumolpus was said to have come from Thrace as the son of Poseidon and Chione, and Homer called him a noble man. His tomb was shown by both the Athenians and Eubœans; he was killed in the battle between the Eleusinians and Athenians through the death of his son Immaradus, and Ceryx was said by heralds not to have been his son.

l: Theseus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Theseus slew the robber Polypemon, surnamed Procrustes, near the Cephisus. He also defeated Cercyon in wrestling by using skill rather than mere strength, and the account says that he was the first to make wrestling a science and later established training schools.

l: Eleusis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Eleusis contained temples to Triptolemus, Propylæan Artemis, and Father Poseidon, as well as the Well of Callichorus and the Rharian plain, which tradition called the first land sown and cultivated. Its name was attributed by different traditions to a hero called Eleusis, and it became associated with Athens after the battle with the Athenians while retaining its Mysteries.

l: Eleusinian mysteries, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: After the battle between Eleusis and Athens, the people of Eleusis remained Athenians in other matters but kept the private management of the Eleusinian Mysteries. The narrator refused to disclose what was inside the sacred wall, saying that the uninitiated were forbidden both to see and to hear about the Mysteries.

l: Bœotia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: As one traveled from Eleusis toward Bœotia, the Platæan district marked the old boundary between the Athenians and the people of Eleutheræ. After Eleutheræ joined Athens, Mount Cithæron in Bœotia became the boundary.

l: Megara, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Megara was said originally to have belonged to the Athenians through Pandion, but the Peloponnesians later took it and gave it to Corinthians and other allies, after which its inhabitants became Dorians in customs and dialect. The unit describes Megara's temples, monuments, rulers, traditions, and competing accounts of its name and early history.

l: Thebes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Creon, ruling Thebes as regent for Laodamas, was said to have refused burial to those who fell in battle, prompting Adrastus to appeal to Theseus and leading to an Athenian-Bœotian conflict. The Thebans instead claimed that they voluntarily surrendered the dead bodies.

l: Pandion, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Pandion was said to have received Megaris from its king Pylas, and his tomb was shown in that district. His son Nisus became king of Megara, and Pandion also had a hero-chapel and divine honors at Megara.

l: Alcathous, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Alcathous, the son of Pelops, killed the lion of Mount Cithæron and thereby received Megareus's daughter and the succession to the kingdom according to local tradition. After becoming king, he built a temple to Huntress Artemis and Hunter Apollo and later rebuilt Megara's wall after the Cretans had destroyed the old one.

l: battle between Eleusis and Athens, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: In the battle between Eleusis and Athens, Erechtheus, king of Athens, and Immaradus, son of Eumolpus, were killed. The resulting peace made the people of Eleusis Athenians in other respects but preserved their private management of the Mysteries.

l: rape of Proserpine, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The rape of Proserpine was associated with Demeter's arrival at the Well of Flowers, where she sat disguised as an old woman. It was also said that Pluto descended at Erineus after carrying Proserpine away.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XLII.
s: The unit describes the sanctuaries, tombs, monuments, and traditions of Megara and its surrounding towns. Alcathous is associated with the building of Megara’s wall, the temples and tombs of his family, and the killing of his son Callipolis. Apollo is said to have helped Alcathous build the wall, leaving his harp on a stone that produces a harp-like sound when struck. Theseus appears in traditions involving Periboea, Timalcus, and the punishment of Sciron.

l: Megara, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XLII.
s: Megara contains a citadel named after Alcathous, temples of Athene, Apollo, Demeter, Dionysus, Aphrodite, and other deities, and numerous tombs and hero-chapels. Its traditions include the claim that Periboea was sent from Megara with Theseus to Crete, that Ino’s body was buried there, and that Iphigenia and Adrastus died there. Megara also possesses the towns and sites of Nisæa, Pagæ, and Ægosthena, and its road toward Corinth includes the Scironian road and the Molurian rock.

l: Alcathous, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XLII.
s: Alcathous is associated with the citadel and wall of Megara, which he began building after sacrificing to the Prodromi gods. Apollo is said to have assisted him, and Alcathous’s daughter Periboea was sent with Theseus to Crete. His sons Ischepolis and Callipolis died tragically: Ischepolis was killed fighting the Calydonian boar, and Alcathous killed Callipolis after mistaking his grief-stricken act at the altar for irreverence.

l: Apollo, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XLII.
s: Apollo is said by the Megarians to have helped Alcathous build the wall of Megara and to have placed his harp on a stone beside the altar of the Prodromi gods. The stone produces a sound like a harp when struck with a pebble. Megara also contains temples and statues of Apollo, including Apollo Pythius, Apollo Decataphorus, Apollo Archegetes, Protecting Apollo, Apollo Carinus, and Latoan Apollo.

l: Theseus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XLII.
s: Theseus took Periboea, the daughter of Alcathous, to Crete in connection with the tribute. A council chamber at Megara was said to have been the tomb of Timalcus, whom Theseus killed. Theseus also threw Sciron into the sea, imposing on him the fate associated with the strangers Sciron had murdered.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: The unit describes Corinth, its mythic origins, Roman destruction and rebuilding, major sanctuaries, monuments, harbours, and traditions. It recounts the Isthmus of Corinth, the Isthmian games, and the temples and statues associated with Poseidon, Aphrodite, Bellerophon, Artemis, Apollo, and Athene. It also traces Corinthian rulers and traditions concerning Medea, Sisyphus, the Bacchidae, and the Dorian conquest. The account concludes with Acrocorinth, its sanctuaries, fountain, and the nearby Teneatic gate and Tenea.

l: Corinth, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: Corinth is said to have taken its name from Corinthus, though Eumelus gives an alternative account involving Ephyre, Marathon, and the Ephyræans. The ancient Corinthians no longer inhabit the city; it was destroyed by the Romans after joining the Achaean revolt and was later rebuilt. The unit describes its temples, market-place, theatre, stadium, baths, fountains, tombs, rulers, and surrounding territory.

l: Romans, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: The Romans conquered the Greeks after the Achaean revolt, took away their arms, and razed the fortifications of their fortified cities. Under Mummius they destroyed Corinth, and Roman colonists later inhabited the rebuilt city.

l: Achaean confederacy, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: The Achaean confederacy included Corinth, which joined its war against the Romans. Critolaus, appointed commander in chief, persuaded the Achaeans and many Greeks outside the Peloponnese to revolt.

l: Poseidon, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: Poseidon was said to have received the Isthmus and the land toward the sea after Briareus arbitrated his dispute with the Sun. Corinth contained temples, statues, altars, and other representations of Poseidon, including a temple at Lechaeum, a statue at Cenchreae, and a sanctuary at the Isthmus.

l: Isthmian games, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: Sisyphus established the Isthmian games in honour of Melicerta after burying him at the Isthmus. The games continued after Corinth was destroyed by Mummius, being held at Sicyon while Corinth lay desolate, and returned to Corinth when the city was rebuilt.

l: Isthmus, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: The Isthmus extends from the sea near Cenchreae to the sea near Lechaeum and makes the Peloponnese a peninsula. Attempts to cut a canal through it failed, and the remains of one excavation were still visible.

l: Cenchreae, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: Cenchreae was one of Corinth's seaports, said to have been named after Cenchrias, the reputed son of Poseidon and Pirene. It contained a temple of Artemis, a shrine of Aphrodite, a brazen statue of Poseidon, and temples of Æsculapius and Isis.

l: Lechaeum, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: Lechaeum was one of Corinth's seaports, said to have been named after Leches, the reputed son of Poseidon and Pirene. It contained a temple and brazen statue of Poseidon.

l: Theatre of Corinth, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: The Theatre was one of the great sights of Corinth. Near it stood the temple of Athene the Bridler, a wooden statue of Hercules attributed to Daedalus, a temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, and an old gymnasium.

l: Aphrodite, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: Aphrodite had a statue in Corinth by Hermogenes of Cythera and a shrine of Melænian Aphrodite in the Craneum grove. On Acrocorinth she had a temple with statues showing her in armour, along with the Sun and Cupid.

l: Bellerophon, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: Bellerophon was honoured at Corinth by a temple in the Craneum grove and appeared on a conduit near the statue of Artemis. Athene the Bridler was said to have helped him, broken and bridled Pegasus, and given the horse to him.

l: Artemis, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: Artemis had an old wooden statue and a temple on the road from the Isthmus to Cenchreae. A temple and statue of Artemis hunting stood near a famous bath, and a conduit in Corinth was decorated with her statue and a figure of Bellerophon.

l: Apollo, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: Apollo was represented by a statue near the well of Pirene and by a statue called the Clarian in the Corinthian market-place. A temple and brazen statue of Apollo stood on the road from Corinth toward Sicyon, and Tenea held Apollo in the highest honour.

l: Athene, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: Athene had a brazen statue in the middle of the Corinthian market-place, with the Muses sculptured on its base. As Athene the Bridler, she had a temple near the Theatre and was said to have aided Bellerophon by giving him Pegasus.

l: Medea, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: Medea was said to have become queen of Corinth after the Corinthians summoned her from Iolcus, and Jason became king through her. Accounts differ about her children and their deaths, but one Corinthian tradition says that she hid her children in Hera's temple, later left Corinth, and handed the kingdom to Sisyphus.

l: Acrocorinth, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: Acrocorinth was the summit above Corinth, which the Corinthians said Briareus awarded to the Sun and the Sun gave to Aphrodite. It contained temples of Isis, Serapis, the Sun, Necessity and Force, the Mother of the Gods, the Fates, Demeter, Proserpine, and Bunæan Hera, as well as a temple of Aphrodite and a fountain associated with Asopus or Pirene.

l: destruction of Corinth by Mummius, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: Mummius, the Roman army's general, destroyed Corinth after the Corinthians participated in the Achaean war against Rome. While the city lay desolate, the Isthmian games were held at Sicyon.

l: rebuilding of Corinth by Julius Caesar, Description of Greece, BOOK II.--CORINTH.
s: Julius Caesar was said to have rebuilt Corinth and instituted the Imperial form of government at Rome. After the rebuilding, the Isthmian games returned to Corinth, and the city was inhabited by Roman colonists.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, And as you go from Corinth along the coast in the direction of Sicyon
s: The text describes a burnt temple near Corinth on the road toward Sicyon, identified by some as a temple of Apollo and by others as a temple of Olympian Zeus. It recounts the Sicyonians’ traditions about Ægialeus, the founding of Ægialea, and the succession of their early kings. It also relates that Demeter saved Plemnæus’s son Orthopolis after Plemnæus’s other children died at birth. Orthopolis’s descendants included Chrysorthe, Coronus, Corax, and Lamedon.

l: Corinth, Description of Greece, And as you go from Corinth along the coast in the direction of Sicyon
s: Corinth is located near the burnt temple on the coastal road toward Sicyon. Several wars have taken place around Corinth, and fires have consumed houses and temples outside its walls; the Corinthians are said either to have built the temple to Olympian Zeus or to have lost it in an accidental fire.

l: Sicyon, Description of Greece, And as you go from Corinth along the coast in the direction of Sicyon
s: Sicyon is near Corinth, and its people preserve traditions about their region and early rulers. They say that Ægialeus founded Ægialea in the plain and that the site of the burnt temple of Apollo was the city’s citadel.

l: temple, Description of Greece, And as you go from Corinth along the coast in the direction of Sicyon
s: The temple stands not far from Corinth on the left side of the road toward Sicyon and has been burnt down. One account identifies it as a temple of Apollo destroyed by Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles; another says that the Corinthians dedicated it to Olympian Zeus and that an accidental fire destroyed it.

l: Ægialeus, Description of Greece, And as you go from Corinth along the coast in the direction of Sicyon
s: Ægialeus is said by the people of Sicyon to have been an Autochthon who first dwelt in their region. Ægialus in the Peloponnese was reportedly named after him, and he founded Ægialea in the plain; the site of the temple of Apollo was said to have been its citadel.

l: genealogy of Sicyon’s kings, Description of Greece, And as you go from Corinth along the coast in the direction of Sicyon
s: The reported succession begins with Ægialeus, followed by his son Europs, Europs’s son Telchis, and Telchis’s son Apis. Apis’s son was Thelxion, followed by Ægyrus, Thurimachus, and Leucippus. Leucippus had only one daughter, Chalcinia, who bore Peratus to Poseidon; Peratus was raised by Leucippus and succeeded him as king. Peratus’s son was Plemnæus, whose son Orthopolis was reared by Demeter; Orthopolis’s daughter was Chrysorthe, whose son was Coronus, father of Corax and Lamedon.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The unit recounts the mythic and historical succession of rulers in Sicyon and the origins of its name, including Epopeus's conflict with Thebes over Antiope and the later Dorian takeover. It describes Sicyon's monuments, tombs, sanctuaries, festivals, religious images, and the earthquake that greatly reduced its population and artistic treasures. It also narrates Aratus's liberation of Sicyon, the city's entry into the Achæan league, and the league's wars with Cleomenes and the Macedonians. The final chapters describe the Battle of Sellasia, the poisoning of Aratus by Philip, and the sanctuaries of Hercules, Æsculapius, Aphrodite, Apollo, and Artemis.

l: Epopeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Epopeus came from Thessaly and obtained the kingdom after Corax died childless. He fought the Thebans over Antiope, won the battle despite being wounded, sacrificed to Athene, built her a temple, and later died from his neglected wound.

l: Antiope, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Antiope, the daughter of Nycteus and reputedly connected with the river Asopus, was renowned for her beauty. Epopeus took or sought to marry her, and while being taken to Thebes she gave birth near Eleutheræ to Zethus and Amphion.

l: Thebes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Thebes sent an army against Epopeus because of Antiope, and Nycteus was wounded in the conflict. The city was later associated with the Theban Phanes, who brought the image of Lysius to Sicyon.

l: Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Zeus was named as the father of Antiope's sons in the verses of Asius. The text also quotes Hesiod concerning Zeus bringing down the pride of many cities.

l: Sicyon, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Sicyon was said by different authorities to be the son of Marathon, Metion, Erechtheus, or Pelops. He became connected with the region and city that were thereafter called Sicyonia and Sicyon.

l: Sicyonia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Sicyonia received its name after Sicyon became king, replacing the earlier name Ægialea. It later became part of Argolis after the Sicyonians became Dorians.

l: Sicyon (city), Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Sicyon was first built by Ægialeus in the plain, while Demetrius the son of Antigonus later destroyed that settlement and built the present city on the former citadel. The city contained numerous temples, tombs, theaters, a market-place, a gymnasium, and sanctuaries dedicated to several gods and heroes.

l: Dionysus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Sicyon had a temple of Dionysus containing a gold-and-ivory image of the god and white-stone figures of Bacchantes. Once each year, secret statues were carried by torchlight from the Ornament Room to the temple in a procession with national hymns.

l: Adrastus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: After fleeing Argos, Adrastus went to Polybus at Sicyon and obtained the chief power there after Polybus died. He later returned to Argos, after which Ianiscus became king of Sicyon.

l: Hercules, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Sicyon had statues and sanctuaries of Hercules, including a stone figure by Scopas and an old wooden image by Laphaes of Phlius. The Sicyonians sacrificed to Hercules both as a hero and, in another part of the festival, as a god.

l: Apollo, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Apollo was worshipped at Sicyon in temples and sanctuaries, including the temple in the market-place and the temple of the Lycian, or Wolf-god, Apollo. The Sicyonians said that Apollo cured the daughters of Prœtus and destroyed wolves by directing that bark and flesh be placed before them.

l: Dorians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Dorians seized Sicyon with Phalces, the son of Temenus, who spared Lacestades because he too was a descendant of Hercules. The Sicyonians subsequently became Dorians and joined the political territory of Argolis.

l: Argolis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Argolis included Sicyon after the Sicyonians became Dorians. The coast of Argolis also included Epidaurus and Trœzen, which later joined the Achæan league.

l: Corinth, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Corinth was held by a Macedonian garrison under Antigonus. Aratus attacked the garrison suddenly, defeated it, and later helped free Corinth.

l: Sellasia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Sellasia was the place where Antigonus and the Achæans defeated Cleomenes. After the victory, Sellasia was enslaved and Lacedæmon was captured.

l: Aratus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Aratus overthrew Nicocles at Sicyon, restored isonomy, and returned the refugees' houses and property with compensation to purchasers. He brought Sicyon into the Achæan league, led campaigns against several enemies, helped free Corinth, and later was poisoned by Philip; his body was buried at Sicyon in the Arateum.

l: Artemis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Artemis was worshipped at Sicyon in several forms, including Artemis Limnæa, the Pheræan Artemis, and a golden Artemis near a statue of Zeus. Her image was carried with Apollo during the annual procession connected with the temple of Persuasion.

l: Achæan league, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Aratus forced Sicyon, despite its Dorian identity, into the Achæan league and became its commander in chief. The league later fought with Cleomenes, defeated him at Sellasia with Antigonus, and expanded when Corinth, Epidaurus, Trœzen, Megara, and Argos joined it.

l: Macedonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Macedonians and Antigonus were feared by the Greeks and held Corinth and the forts of the Piræus, Munychia, Salamis, and Sunium. Aratus opposed their power but eventually became their ally, and the Macedonian influence was involved in his death.

l: Philip, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Philip took control after Antigonus and murdered Aratus by secretly giving him poison because Aratus criticized his violent conduct toward his subjects. Philip also poisoned the Athenian orators Euryclides and Micon, and later suffered grief when his son Demetrius was poisoned by Perseus.

l: Argos, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Argos was ruled by Aristomachus when Aratus persuaded him to establish a democracy and join the Achæan league. Adrastus had earlier ruled at Sicyon after fleeing Argos and later returned there.

l: Sparta, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Sparta was ruled by Cleomenes, who sought autocratic power and attacked the Achæans. After his defeat and flight to Egypt, the Spartans abandoned kingly government and retained a republican form.

l: Cleomenes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Cleomenes became king in Sparta, removed Eurydamidas by poison, curtailed the authority of the Ephors and Senate, and attacked the Achæans. Antigonus and the Achæans defeated him at Sellasia; he fled to Egypt, later escaped from prison, caused trouble at Alexandria, and killed himself when captured.

l: Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Lacedæmonians and Agis seized Pellene but withdrew after Aratus defeated them. Antigonus and the Achæans later restored their old political constitution after capturing Lacedæmon.

l: Æsculapius, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Sicyon possessed a temple of Æsculapius with a gold-and-ivory beardless image by Calamis. The Sicyonians said that the god came from Epidaurus in the form of a dragon and that Aratus was his son through Aristodama.

l: Aphrodite, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Aphrodite had a sanctuary at Sicyon containing a gold-and-ivory seated image by Canachus. Only a maiden sacristan and a maiden bath-carrier performed rites inside, while others worshipped the goddess from the porch.

l: Sicyonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Sicyonians preserved traditions about their rulers, foundations, tombs, temples, festivals, and sacred images. They became Dorians, joined the Achæan league under Aratus, and suffered a devastating earthquake that left the city nearly depopulated and destroyed many works of art.

l: Sicyonian royal succession, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The succession passed from Epopeus to Lamedon, who gave Antiope up to Thebes and married Pheno from Athens. Later rulers included Sicyon, Polybus, Adrastus, Ianiscus, Phæstus, Zeuxippus, Hippolytus, and Lacestades, before Phalces shared power with Lacestades after the Dorian seizure.

l: Sicyonian earthquake, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: An earthquake struck Sicyon when the city's fortunes were already poor. It made the city almost bare of inhabitants and destroyed many works of art, while also damaging cities in Caria and Lycia and especially Rhodes.

l: Aratus's liberation of Sicyon, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Aratus entered Sicyon at night with Sicyonian refugees and mercenaries from Argos, overcame the garrison, and forced Nicocles to flee. He restored isonomy and returned the refugees' houses and goods with compensation to those who had purchased them.

l: Cleomenes' war with the Achæans, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Cleomenes attacked the Achæans and defeated them at Dyme while Aratus was their general. His subsequent violation of agreements, including the expulsion of the inhabitants of Megalopolis, led Aratus to seek Antigonus's aid against him.

l: Battle of Sellasia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: At Sellasia, Antigonus and the Achæans defeated Cleomenes after Cleomenes violated his terms with Antigonus. Sellasia was enslaved, Lacedæmon was captured, and the old political order of the Lacedæmonians was restored.

l: poisoning of Aratus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Philip secretly poisoned Aratus because Aratus criticized and sometimes restrained his violent behavior toward his subjects. Aratus died at Ægium, and his body was taken to Sicyon for burial in the hero-chapel called the Arateum.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Epopeus is associated with a former shrine of Athene and with temples and altars near Sicyon, while Adrastus is credited with building temples and altars to several deities. The account describes sanctuaries of Demeter, Artemis, Apollo, Hera, and the Eumenides around Sicyon, as well as the road from Sicyon to Titane. Titan is said to have first dwelt at Titane and to have been regarded as the Sun’s brother because of his knowledge of the seasons. At Titane, Alexanor built a temple of Æsculapius, whose precinct contains statues and sacred objects connected with Æsculapius, Hygiea, and other figures.

l: Epopeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Epopeus formerly erected a shrine of Athene that surpassed those of its time in size and beauty, but time obscured its fame. Lightning struck the shrine, leaving only its altar; his tomb stood in front of the altar, near the Gods the Averters of Evil.

l: Adrastus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Adrastus built the temple next to Hera’s temple, as well as altars to Pan and the Sun God behind Hera’s temple. No statues remained in the temple he built next to Hera.

l: Demeter, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Demeter had a temple on the descent to the plain, said to have been built by Plemnæus in gratitude for her rearing his son. She also had a temple in the grove called Pyræa, where she was worshipped with Proserpine, and her statue was present in the Nymphon.

l: Sicyon, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Sicyon was the starting point for roads to Phlius and Titane. Near Sicyon were temples and groves dedicated to Demeter, Proserpine, and the Eumenides, whom the Sicyonians called the Eumenides and worshipped with sacrifices, libations, and flowers.

l: Titane, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Titane was reached by a narrow road from Sicyon and lay beyond the Asopus. It contained a mountain-top where the natives said Titan first dwelt, and it later became the site of Alexanor’s temple of Æsculapius.

l: Titan, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Titan was said by the natives to have first dwelt on the mountain-top at Titane and to have given the place its name. He was regarded as the Sun’s brother because he was thought to have been exceptionally skilled in observing the seasons when the Sun fructified and ripened seeds and fruit.

l: Alexanor, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Alexanor, the son of Machaon and grandson of Æsculapius, came to Sicyon and built the temple of Æsculapius at Titane. A statue of Alexanor stood within the precinct, and sacrifices were offered to him after sunset as to a hero.

l: Æsculapius, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Æsculapius was worshipped at Titane in a temple built by Alexanor. His statue’s material and maker were unknown, though some attributed it to Alexanor; only its face, fingers, and toes were visible beneath a white woollen tunic and cloak. A stone statue described as Gortynian Æsculapius also stood in the porch.

l: temple of Æsculapius at Titane, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The temple was built by Alexanor, son of Machaon and grandson of Æsculapius, and its precinct contained a few inhabitants, mostly suppliants of the god, along with old cypress trees. It held partially concealed statues of Æsculapius and Hygiea, statues of Alexanor and Euamerion, a wooden statue of Coronis, and other wooden and stone figures; sacred dragons also lived within the precinct.

l: Hygiea, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Hygiea had a statue at the temple of Æsculapius at Titane that was difficult to see because women’s shorn hair and the folds of a Babylonish garment concealed it. Whoever wished to propitiate either Hygiea or Æsculapius was instructed to worship Hygiea.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: The unit describes the traditions, sanctuaries, and history of Phliasia and Phlius, including the origins of Aras, Aræthyrea, Phlias, and the mysteries at Celeæ. It recounts the arrival of the Dorians under Rhegnidas, the resistance of Hippasus, and the later fame of Pythagoras. It then traces the roads and sacred places around Cleonæ, Nemea, Argos, Mycenæ, Tiryns, and the temple of Hera. The account includes traditions concerning Perseus, Acrisius, Zeus, Demeter, Hebe, Dysaules, and Hera.

l: Phliasia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Phliasia lies next to Sicyonia, and its chief town is Phlius. The Phliasians are said to have been originally Argives and to have become Dorians after the return of the Heraclidæ.

l: Phlius, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Phlius is at most 40 stades from Titane, with a straight road from Sicyon. Its traditions, sanctuaries, monuments, and public buildings include the citadel, the temple and grove of Hebe, precincts of Demeter, temples of Æsculapius, Dionysus, Apollo, and Isis, and the house associated with Amphiaraus.

l: Phliasians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: The Phliasians say that Aras was the first person to live in their land and that he founded the city formerly called Arantia. They preserve traditions about Aras, Aoris, Aræthyrea, Phlias, Dysaules, and the mysteries at Celeæ, and they honor Hebe by granting immunity to slaves who seek refuge in her precinct.

l: Dorians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Dorians entered Phlius under Rhegnidas, who demanded that they and he receive lands and that he become king. Some Phliasians accepted these terms, while others resisted.

l: Heraclidæ, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: The return of the Heraclidæ disturbed the Peloponnese, except Arcadia, and caused many cities to receive Dorian settlers and undergo changes of inhabitants. Phliasia is said to have become Dorian after their return.

l: Aras, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Aras is described as an Autochthon and the first person to live in the land of Phlius. He founded a city on the Arantine hill, gave his name to the land and city called Arantia, and was the father of Aoris and Aræthyrea; his tomb is at Celeæ.

l: Hebe, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Hebe is identified by later Phliasians with the goddess originally called Ganymeda. Her precinct at Phlius includes a cypress grove and an ancient temple, and slaves who come there as suppliants receive complete immunity.

l: Phlias, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Phlias is said to have given his name to the land and to have been the son of Dionysus and Aræthyrea. He was regarded as one of those who sailed in the Argo, and he was married to Chthonophyle, by whom he had Andromedas.

l: Rhegnidas, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Rhegnidas, a Dorian and son of Phalces, marched against Phlius from Argos and Sicyon. He demanded kingship and the assignment of land to himself and the Dorians.

l: Hippasus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Hippasus led those Phliasians who favored vigorous resistance to Rhegnidas and opposed surrendering their advantages to the Dorians. He and his supporters fled to Samos when the people chose the opposing policy.

l: Pythagoras, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Pythagoras, surnamed the Wise, was the great-grandson of Hippasus. His ancestry is given as Hippasus, Euphron, Mnesarchus, and Pythagoras.

l: Hera, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Hera has temples and statues at Phlius, Cleonæ, and especially near Mycenæ. Her great temple near Mycenæ contains a gold-and-ivory statue by Polycletus, and traditions there concern her nurses, her marriage with Zeus, her association with the cuckoo and peacock, and the burning of an older temple.

l: Demeter, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Demeter has precincts and statues at Phlius, and an ancient temple near the citadel. At Celeæ the Phliasians celebrate mysteries of Demeter every fourth year, which they admit are generally an imitation of the Eleusinian mysteries.

l: Celeæ, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Celeæ lies about five stades from Phlius. The Phliasians hold their mysteries of Demeter there every fourth year, and the place contains the tombs of Aras and Dysaules.

l: Dysaules, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Dysaules is said by the Phliasians to have been the brother of Celeus and to have established the mysteries at Celeæ after coming from Eleusis. The account questions whether he was actually driven from Eleusis by Ion, but accepts that he may have come to Celeæ for another reason; his tomb is there.

l: Cleonæ, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Cleonæ is a small town on the road from Corinth to Argos. It contains a temple of Athene with a statue attributed to Scyllis and Dipœnus, and a tomb of Eurytus and Cteatus.

l: Nemea, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Nemea lies about 15 stades from Cleonæ and contains a temple and grove of Nemean Zeus, the tomb and precinct of Opheltes, and a fountain called Adrastea. The Argives sacrifice to Zeus there and hold a winter contest in running for men in armor.

l: Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Zeus is honored at Nemea, where the Argives sacrifice to Nemean Zeus and select his priest. Zeus also appears in traditions at the temple of Hera, including the story that he changed himself into a cuckoo while courting Hera.

l: Mycenæ, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Mycenæ was founded by Perseus after he exchanged kingdoms with Megapenthes, either because his sword scabbard fell there or because he found a fungus and water. The Argives later destroyed it out of jealousy, although its people had sent 80 men to Thermopylæ; ruins, the gate with lions, tombs, and underground treasuries remained.

l: Argos, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Argos was named after Argos, the daughter’s son of Phoroneus, and later became the kingdom of Acrisius. Perseus exchanged it with Megapenthes after unintentionally killing Acrisius, and the Argives eventually destroyed Mycenæ.

l: Acrisius, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Acrisius, son of Abas, retained Argos when he and his brother Prœtus divided the kingdom. He later went to Larissa, where Perseus unintentionally killed him with a quoit, fulfilling the prophecy that he had tried to avert.

l: Tiryns, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Tiryns belonged to the kingdom of Prœtus, and remains of his palace were still visible there. Its walls were said to have been built by the Cyclopes.

l: Perseus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
