s: Perseus unintentionally killed his grandfather Acrisius at Larissa while displaying his skill with quoits. Ashamed of the deed, he exchanged kingdoms with Megapenthes and founded Mycenæ, whose name was explained either by his fallen sword scabbard or by a fungus he found there.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The passage describes landmarks on the road from Mycenæ to Argos, including the hero-chapel of Perseus, the tomb of Thyestes, Mysia, the river Inachus, and the gate of Ilithyia. It recounts how the Argives came to be divided into three kingdoms and traces the succession of rulers until Orestes united Argos and Sparta. It then describes the return of the Heraclidæ to the Peloponnese, their claim to Argos and Messenia, and the displacement of Tisamenus and other ruling families. Tisamenus and his army went to Achaia, while other descendants of Neleus went to Athens.

l: Argos, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Argos was reached by a road from Mycenæ marked by the tomb of Thyestes, Mysia, the river Inachus, and the gate of Ilithyia. Its kingdom was once divided among three royal lines, but Orestes eventually acquired Argos and ruled it together with Sparta. The Heraclidæ later expelled Tisamenus from Argos.

l: Argives, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Argives said that Mysius had been a host of Demeter and that their people had once been divided into three kingdoms. They also preserved traditions about the succession of kings and about the Heraclidæ’s return and claims in the Peloponnese.

l: three Argive kingdoms, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The three Argive kingdoms arose during the reign of Anaxagoras after Melampus cured a madness affecting the women, in return for sharing the rule with his brother Bias. The native line descended from Anaxagoras, the line of Bias, and the line of Melampus supplied the three royal successions until Cylarabes became sole king.

l: Orestes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Orestes, the son of Agamemnon, acquired Argos after Cylarabes died childless. He had also gained much Arcadian territory and the kingdom of Sparta, whose people accepted him as king because they preferred the descendants of Tyndareus’ daughters to Menelaus’ sons by a bondmaid.

l: Sparta, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Sparta came under the rule of Orestes after the Lacedæmonians requested him as king. The Heraclidæ later turned Tisamenus out of Lacedæmon and Argos.

l: Tisamenus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Tisamenus, the son of Orestes and Hermione, succeeded Orestes as king. During his reign the Heraclidæ returned to the Peloponnese, expelled him from Lacedæmon and Argos, and drove him and his sons to Achaia with their army.

l: Heraclidæ, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Heraclidæ returned to the Peloponnese during the reign of Tisamenus, led by Temenus and Cresphontes and by the sons of Aristodemus. They expelled Tisamenus from Lacedæmon and Argos and the descendants of Nestor from Messenia.

l: Peloponnese, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Heraclidæ returned to the Peloponnese during the reign of Tisamenus. They claimed Argos and Messenia and displaced the ruling descendants of Pelops and Nestor.

l: claim of the Heraclidæ to Argos, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Heraclidæ claimed Argos on the ground that Tisamenus was descended from Pelops, whereas they descended from Perseus. They further argued that Hercules had killed Hippocoon and his sons and restored the country to Tyndareus, supporting their claim to the region.

l: Messenia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Heraclidæ claimed Messenia by arguing that Hercules had entrusted it to Nestor when he took Pylos. They expelled the descendants of Nestor, including Alcmæon, Pisistratus, the sons of Pæon, and Melanthus.

l: Achaia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Tisamenus and his sons went to what was then called Achaia with their army after the Heraclidæ expelled them from Lacedæmon and Argos.

l: Athens, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The descendants of Neleus other than Pisistratus went to Athens after being displaced from the Peloponnese. The Pæonidæ and Alcmæonidæ were said to have been named after them, and Melanthus became king of Athens after expelling Thymœtes.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Temenus made Deiphontes his general and associate, married him to his daughter Hyrnetho, and was killed by his sons, after which the Argives gradually reduced and then abolished the kingly power. The unit describes Argive temples, tombs, statues, votive offerings, and local traditions concerning Danaus, Hypermnestra, Apollo, Zeus, and other figures. It recounts conflicts involving the Argives, the Lacedæmonians, Cleomenes, Perseus, and Poseidon, including the defense of Argos led by Telesilla and the flooding of the Argive land. It also gives competing accounts of Medusa and the Gorgon and discusses the origins and memorials of several Argive heroes and institutions.

l: Temenus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Temenus appointed Deiphontes general in his battles, made him his associate in all things, and gave him his daughter Hyrnetho in marriage. Because he seemed likely to make Hyrnetho and Deiphontes his heirs, his sons killed him.

l: Deiphontes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Deiphontes, the son of Antimachus and a descendant of Hercules, served as Temenus's general and associate. He married Hyrnetho, whom Temenus favored above his other children.

l: Argives, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The Argives reduced the power of their kings until Medon and his descendants retained only the royal title, and they later deprived Meltas of his kingdom. They built and maintained numerous temples, tombs, statues, and memorials in their city, fought repeatedly with the Lacedæmonians, and were defended by Telesilla and the women of Argos against Cleomenes.

l: Argos, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Argos contains the temples, tombs, monuments, and market-place described throughout the unit. It was left nearly without men after Cleomenes and the Lacedæmonians defeated the Argives, but Telesilla organized its defense.
